To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Z/super 0/ mass is not shifted excessively by mixing with a heavy neutral vector bosons, that the mixing angle is bounded by the Higgs structure of the mass matrices, and that these bounds are compared with those from neutral current experiments.
the Z/super 0/ mass is not significantly shifted from the standard value by mixing with an extra neutral vector boson Z' with a mass of 500 GeV or less.
the Z' mass is constrained by the Higgs vacuum structure to lie between about 200 GeV and 1 TeV for a wide range of mixing angles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the physics of a new neutral heavy gauge boson Z/sup 1/ in the context of an extended gauge model.
the effects of a new heavy gauge boson, Z', on e/sup +-/e/sup +/ physics at SLAC and LEP.
the study of the effects of a new heavy Z' boson at SLE and LEP.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in spite of a great effort, the physics community has not yet succeeded in finding a convincing and unambiguous way to determine the quark masses, and that the present situation is not very promising.
, while the LEP data do not yet rule out a Z' boson, they do provide a very stringent limit on any Z' boson that is accessible to the LEP experiments.
the present data are consistent with the standard model, and that no significant deviation is observed from it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Z' is excluded at the 95% confidence level in all models except those with very small Z'-Z mixing and Z' masses below 10 GeV.
the Z'/Z mixing angle must be less than 0.1 degrees for the Z' mass to be less than 100 GeV/c/sup 2/.
there is no new physics in the neutral current sector at SLC or LEP.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a Z' boson could be discovered at LEP or SLC, and that it would have a very large effect on the physics of e/sup +/-e/sup -/.
the Z' mass can be as low as 50 GeV and still not be excluded by the current data, and that the SLC and LHC will be able to discover it if it exists.
